The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional weight of the narrative. In terms of "story time," the entire scene takes place over just a couple of minutes—between the last car rolling off the ferry and Ilse untying the rope to cross again. The author stretches this brief moment by weaving Ilse's internal observations, sensory details (the sound of the water, the singing of the rope), and unspoken history into the pauses between sparse dialogue. This stretching of time mirrors the sluggishness of the brown river and the heavy, awkward silence between two estranged family members. 

Simultaneously, the author uses extreme compression to convey decades of backstory and routine without breaking the rhythm of the present scene. Years of labor are compressed into a single clause ("wenn man jahrzehntelang an ihm gearbeitet hatte"), and a lifetime of family history is condensed into a single observation about Jonas having "Hennings Stirn." Even a hypothetical future is briefly compressed and discarded when Ilse imagines Jonas walking up the gravel path alone. This balance between the stretched, tense present and the compressed weight of the past makes the final gesture of reconciliation feel earned and deeply resonant.
